summary: Describes extensions to RSVP-TE for setting up traffic-engineered point-to-multipoint label switched paths in MPLS and GMPLS networks. The approach relies on RSVP-TE alone and does not need a multicast routing protocol in the provider core. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: One sender needs to deliver the same message to many receivers along planned paths. This note shows how a network builds a tree of routes without using a separate group-sending system.

questions: how to set up p2mp te lsps
how does p2mp lsp grafting and pruning work
subtitle: How RSVP-TE builds traffic-engineered trees from one sender to many receivers, with no multicast routing protocol in the core.

tldr.problem: RSVP-TE (RFC 3209) and its GMPLS extension (RFC 3473) only set up point-to-point LSPs, so there was no way to build a traffic-engineered LSP that delivers the same data to several destinations.
tldr.mechanism: A P2MP LSP is made of many source-to-leaf (S2L) sub-LSPs that share a SESSION object and are signaled in one or more Path messages. Branch nodes replicate data, and Sub-Group fields tell apart the Path messages that carry parts of the same tree.
tldr.outcome: P2MP TE LSPs can be built, grown, pruned, re-optimized and protected using RSVP-TE alone. RFC 6510 later updated this RFC.

today: RFC 4875 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 6510.

sections.title: Point-to-Multipoint TE LSPs
sections.content:
RFC 3209 sets up point-to-point traffic-engineered (TE) label switched paths in MPLS networks, and RFC 3473 does the same for GMPLS. Neither can build a point-to-multipoint (P2MP) LSP. This RFC extends RSVP-TE to do so, meeting the requirements in RFC 4461.

The design optimizes replication by letting non-ingress nodes act as replication or branch nodes: a branch LSR copies incoming labeled data onto one or more outgoing interfaces, which may use different labels. It relies on RSVP-TE itself, with no multicast routing protocol in the service provider core.

How applications use P2MP TE LSPs and how paths are computed are outside the scope of the document.
sections.eli5: Normal routes go from one place to one other place. This note teaches routers to build routes shaped like a tree, so one sender can reach many receivers.

sections.title: Tunnels, LSPs and Sub-LSPs
sections.content:
A P2MP TE tunnel is identified by a P2MP SESSION object holding a P2MP ID (a four-octet number unique within the ingress LSR), a Tunnel ID and an Extended Tunnel ID. It is the SESSION of RFC 3209 with the Tunnel Endpoint Address replaced by the P2MP ID. The tunnel holds one or more P2MP LSPs, each identified by the SESSION plus the tunnel sender address and LSP ID in a P2MP SENDER_TEMPLATE object.

A P2MP LSP is made of S2L sub-LSPs, one per leaf. Each is identified by the P2MP LSP plus the destination address in an S2L_SUB_LSP object. One Path message may signal one or many S2L sub-LSPs, and a P2MP LSP may use several Path messages, because one message may not be large enough and because separate messages let the ingress manage sub-trees on their own.

To tell such Path messages apart, SENDER_TEMPLATE and FILTER_SPEC gain a Sub-Group Originator ID and a Sub-Group ID. The originator is the TE Router ID of the LSR that originates the Path message; the Sub-Group ID space is specific to that originator. Sub-groups describe signaling state only, not data replication. They are used to add an egress and to split state so a Path message fits within a single IP packet.

The RFC defines new objects: SESSION C-Types 13 (IPv4) and 14 (IPv6), SENDER_TEMPLATE and FILTER_SPEC C-Types 12 and 13, an S2L_SUB_LSP object of class 50 (C-Types 1 and 2), and C-Type 2 for the secondary explicit and record route objects defined in RFC 4873.
sections.eli5: The whole tree has a name tag. Each branch to one receiver is a small piece of the tree, and when the message is too big for one envelope, the pieces are numbered so nobody mixes them up.

sections.title: Explicit Routes and Compression
sections.content:
If a Path message signals one S2L sub-LSP, the EXPLICIT_ROUTE object (ERO) holds the path to that egress; without it, hop-by-hop routing toward the S2L_SUB_LSP destination is used. The ERO plus S2L_SUB_LSP form the sub-LSP descriptor.

If a Path message signals several sub-LSPs, the ERO carries the path of the first one. Each later one gets a P2MP SECONDARY_EXPLICIT_ROUTE object (SERO) holding only the path from a branch LSR to that egress. The branch MUST appear as an explicit hop in the ERO or another SERO. This explicit route compression avoids repeating shared hops, reduces Path message size and cuts extra processing.

Every LSR processes the ERO of the first sub-LSP. It handles a later sub-LSP only when the first hop of that SERO is one of its own addresses, and a branch LSR propagates only the relevant descriptors on each downstream link. A subsequent sub-LSP can therefore become the first one in an outgoing message. In the RFC's Figure 1, LSR A signals six egresses (F, N, O, P, Q, R), and when LSR E splits the message toward D and H, each outgoing message re-encodes its own ERO and SEROs.
sections.eli5: Instead of every receiver getting a full set of directions from the start, only the junctions that split the path need the extra directions, so the message stays short.

sections.title: Path and Resv Message Handling
sections.content:
An LSR that supports P2MP MUST handle multiple Path messages for the same P2MP LSP and multiple S2L sub-LSPs in one message. If an LSR cannot support one sub-LSP, it sends a PathErr for that sub-LSP and processing of the rest SHOULD continue. By default other branches still set up and the PathErr does not set Path_State_Removed.

If a transit LSR must split a Path message (for example when ERO expansion makes it overflow), it MUST avoid IP fragmentation. It sends several Path messages with its own TE Router ID as Sub-Group Originator ID and distinct Sub-Group IDs. Apart from the sub-LSP descriptors and hop information, the messages SHOULD be identical.

On the way back, the egress sends a Resv with a label and each node upstream allocates its own label. Resv messages list sub-LSPs in an S2L sub-LSP flow descriptor list, with a P2MP_SECONDARY_RECORD_ROUTE object for each later sub-LSP. A node MUST NOT send a Resv upstream until it has received at least one from downstream. Sub-LSPs of the same P2MP LSP on the same Resv MUST be given the same label, and sub-LSPs of different P2MP LSPs, which differ in sender address or LSP ID, MUST get different labels. Branch nodes SHOULD combine Resv state from several receivers, and MAY send more than one Resv if it would overflow.

To avoid floods of Resv messages when sub-LSPs first come up, a branch node SHOULD delay a Resv whose only change is in SRROs. A suggested delay is thirty seconds, and delays SHOULD generally be longer than 1 second. Notify and ResvConf messages are handled by rewriting Notify node or receiver addresses and Sub-Group fields at nodes that set their own Sub-Group Originator ID, and they MUST be replicated at branch nodes only toward branches that asked for them.
sections.eli5: The request goes down the tree and the answers come back up. Each junction waits for at least one answer before replying, and joins several answers into one reply when it can.

sections.title: Adding, Removing and Re-optimizing Leaves
sections.content:
Adding egresses is called grafting. One way is to add sub-LSPs to an existing Path message and refresh it, which may force the compression to be recomputed. The other is incremental: signal only the new sub-LSPs in a new Path message with a new Sub-Group ID. This keeps Path messages idempotent and avoids tracking expiry of individual sub-LSPs.

Removing egresses is pruning. Implicit teardown sends a modified Path or Resv that lists all sub-LSPs not being removed. Explicit teardown sends a PathTear naming the SESSION, SENDER_TEMPLATE and the Sub-Group tuple of the Path message, which SHOULD be used when all egresses of a Path message are removed. When the ingress removes the whole P2MP LSP, a PathTear MUST be sent for each Path message used.

A node may combine several Path messages into one. The sub-LSP SHOULD stay advertised in both old and new messages until a Resv for the new one arrives, and then it SHOULD be deleted from the old state.

To change paths, the ingress can use make-before-break with a new LSP ID for every sub-LSP, which re-signals the whole P2MP LSP. Alternatively, any node can do sub-group-based re-optimization with new Sub-Group IDs, which may cause transient data duplication. ADMIN_STATUS changes are relayed on every branch, and when R is set, a branch waits for matching responses on all branches before replying upstream.
sections.eli5: Growing the tree means adding new twigs without rebuilding the old branches. Trimming means snipping a twig, and moving a branch means building the new one first before cutting the old one.

sections.title: Branch Failures and Re-Merge
sections.content:
PathErr and ResvErr processing follows RSVP-TE, and an error for one sub-LSP changes only that sub-LSP. The ingress may ask for LSP integrity by setting bit 3 of the Attributes Flags TLV, preferably in the LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES object of RFC 4420. Then a failure on any branch brings down the entire P2MP LSP: the branch LSR sends PathTear on the other branches and PathErr upstream with Path_State_Removed set. A branch that does not support integrity MUST reject with "Routing Error"/"Unsupported LSP Integrity".

Re-merge happens when a branch intersects the same P2MP LSP farther down the tree, for example because of a path calculation or configuration error, and data would be duplicated. Cross-over is similar, but the intersecting branch uses a different outgoing interface, which may be needed in a transparent optical network where different wavelengths reach different leaves.

A node detects this when a Path message for matching state arrives on a different incoming interface. If the sets of S2L_SUB_LSP objects intersect, it is dynamic re-routing. Otherwise it is re-merge or cross-over, and re-merge exists if the outgoing interfaces also intersect. A node MUST support two approaches, selectable by configuration: let the re-merge persist while dropping data from all but one incoming interface, or signal a PathErr ("P2MP Re-Merge Detected") so that the node that created it moves the sub-LSPs away.
sections.eli5: If one twig breaks, you can either leave the rest of the tree alone or throw away the whole tree, depending on what the sender asked for. If two branches grow back together, one of them has to be trimmed so the message is not delivered twice.

sections.title: Fast Reroute and Legacy Routers
sections.content:
Fast reroute from RFC 4090 can protect P2MP LSPs in packet networks, and each S2L sub-LSP of a P2MP LSP MUST have the same protection characteristics. With facility backup, a bypass tunnel protects the link between the point of local repair (PLR) and the next hop, and label stacking sends each P2MP LSP's data through it. For node protection the PLR SHOULD use one or more P2P bypass tunnels, each ending at a downstream merge point; P2MP bypass tunnels are left for further study. With one-to-one backup, backup sub-LSPs are identified with a DETOUR object, and all sub-LSPs of a P2MP LSP between the PLR and next hop MUST be protected. The merge point MUST identify sub-LSPs by LSP-ID and S2L_SUB_LSP object, not by the Sub-Group tuple.

An LSR that understands the extensions but cannot branch in the data plane MUST answer a request to branch with "Routing Error"/"Unable to Branch". An LSR that does not support the extensions will reject the Path message because it does not recognize the SESSION C-Type. Legacy LSRs can still act as transit nodes by LSP stitching and LSP hierarchy: a P2P LSP segment crosses them, and the P2MP Path message is sent to the next P2MP-capable LSR as a directed Path message. Ingress, branch and egress LSRs MUST support the extensions. Transit nodes along the segment do not process the P2MP control messages, which also reduces control plane processing.
sections.eli5: If a road part breaks, traffic can use a ready-made bypass. Routers that do not understand trees can still carry the traffic through a tunnel, as long as the junctions at both ends understand.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
In principle the RFC introduces no new security issues beyond those in RFC 3209, RFC 3473 and RFC 4206. The hop-by-hop integrity mechanisms of RFC 2205 apply to the signaling, and RFC 3473 and RFC 4206 cover the non hop-by-hop signaling used for the legacy-LSR and hierarchy cases.

An administration can limit the domain over which P2MP TE tunnels are established by filtering RSVP Path messages with a P2MP SESSION object. The ingress learns its leaves from the application, so applications MUST give the ingress a way to learn the right leaves, and IETF application specifications MUST describe that mechanism well enough for vendors to interoperate.
sections.eli5: The same locks that protect normal routes protect the tree. Network operators can also block tree requests at their borders if they do not want them.
